items.title: George Masso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: I didn’t listen to Louis Armstrong until years later.

ctx.x: It was his personality. If you were to design a course, a jazz history course, would there be things that you would emphasize? You mentioned active listening. Maybe that’s more my question. What does active listening mean to you?

Well I guess it means listening and making judgments as you go along on what you like — say oh listen to that chorus, listen to what Lester does in this particular phrase, or gee, I don’t know why so and so did that. Listening to the music for what’s inside of it. As far as jazz history, I really don’t feel competent to be able to get into that because I’m as guilty as a lot of other musicians in that when I started to play, that’s where I started to listen. I didn’t go back. I didn’t listen to Louis Armstrong…
have when I first started to play. He had so much to say and so many of those player, Bix Beiderbecke and players in the early twenties.
